title: Modal Verbs
rawText: Modal verbs: können, müssen, dürfen, wollen, sollen, möchten

vocabulary.exampleTranslation: We want to travel to Berlin.
You are supposed to do the homework.
I would like a coffee, please.

grammarTopics.title: Modal Verb Position
grammarTopics.rule: The modal verb takes the second position in the sentence, and the main verb moves to the END in its infinitive form.
grammarTopics.tip: Modal verb = position 2, main verb = end of sentence!

grammarTopics.title: Conjugation (Present Tense)
grammarTopics.rule: Modal verbs are irregular. The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same and have no ending.
grammarTopics.tip: Ich and er/sie/es look the same — no extra ending needed!

exampleSentences.english: He would like to become a doctor.

quizQuestions.question: What does 'können' mean?
quizQuestions.explanation: Können expresses ability — being able to do something.

quizQuestions.question: Where does the main verb go with a modal verb?
quizQuestions.correctAnswer: At the end of the sentence
options: At the end of the sentence
quizQuestions.explanation: With modal verbs, the main verb (infinitive) always goes to the END!

quizQuestions.question: Which modal verb means 'may / to be allowed to'?
quizQuestions.explanation: Dürfen is used to express permission.

quizQuestions.question: Which is correct: 'Ich ___ Deutsch sprechen' (can)?
quizQuestions.explanation: For ich/er/sie/es, können becomes 'kann' — no ending!

quizQuestions.question: What does 'möchten' mean?
quizQuestions.explanation: Möchten is the polite form — use it when ordering or requesting things.

toMemorize: The 6 modal verbs: können, müssen, dürfen, wollen, sollen, möchten
Modal verb goes in position 2; main verb (infinitive) goes to the END
Ich and er/sie/es forms are the same for most modals
können → kann, müssen → muss, dürfen → darf, wollen → will, sollen → soll
toUnderstand: Each modal has a specific meaning — dürfen = permission, müssen = obligation
The difference between wollen (want) and möchten (would like)
Why the infinitive goes to the end (verb bracket structure)

homework.question: Fill in the blank: 'Er ___ morgen zur Schule gehen.' (must)
homework.hint: Which modal verb means must/have to? Think about what form goes with er/sie/es.
homework.explanation: Müssen conjugates to 'muss' for er/sie/es. The sentence means 'He must go to school tomorrow.' Notice 'gehen' stays as infinitive at the end.

homework.question: Translate: 'May I come in?'
homework.hint: Which modal expresses permission? For questions in German, the modal verb comes first.
homework.explanation: Dürfen means 'may / to be allowed to'. In yes/no questions the modal comes first, then the subject. Hereinkommen = to come in.

title: Food Vocabulary

grammarTopics.title: German Articles (der, die, das)
grammarTopics.rule: Every German noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). You must memorize the article with every noun.
grammarTopics.tip: Always learn: 'das Brot' not just 'Brot'. The article IS part of the word!

exampleSentences.german: Zum Frühstück esse ich Brot mit Käse.
exampleSentences.english: For breakfast I eat bread with cheese.

exampleSentences.german: Das Gemüse ist frisch und lecker.
exampleSentences.english: The vegetables are fresh and tasty.
Would you like milk or water?

quizQuestions.question: What is the article for 'Brot' (bread)?
quizQuestions.explanation: Brot (bread) is neuter in German, so its article is 'das'.

quizQuestions.question: What is the article for 'Milch' (milk)?
quizQuestions.explanation: Milch (milk) is feminine in German — die Milch.

quizQuestions.question: How do you say 'the cheese' in German?

toMemorize: das Brot (bread), die Milch (milk), der Käse (cheese)
das Fleisch (meat), das Gemüse (vegetables), die Frucht (fruit)
Always memorize the article WITH the noun
toUnderstand: Why German nouns have genders and why it matters
How articles change in different cases (nominative vs accusative)
